# wbCorr: Bivariate Within- and Between-Cluster Correlations

<!-- badges: start -->
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/wbCorr)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=wbCorr)
[![CRAN downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/wbCorr)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=wbCorr)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/wbCorr/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/wbCorr/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![DOI](https://img.shields.io/badge/DOI-10.5281%2Fzenodo.20357592-blue.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20357592)
<!-- badges: end -->

`wbCorr` computes within- and between-cluster correlations for clustered data,
such as daily diary data with repeated measures nested in persons, or data from
dyads and teams.

In such data, two variables can be related in two ways:

- **Within clusters:** When a person scores higher than usual on one variable,
  do they also score higher than usual on the other?
- **Between clusters:** Do persons with a higher average on one variable also
  have a higher average on the other?

These two correlations can differ in size and even in sign. A correlation over
all rows mixes them. `wbCorr` reports both separately, with p-values, confidence
intervals, and intraclass correlations (ICCs).

If you use `wbCorr`, please cite it as:

`r citation_text`

## Installation

Install the released version from CRAN:

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages("wbCorr")
```

Install the development version:

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages(
  "wbCorr",
  repos = c(
    "https://pascal-kueng.r-universe.dev",
    "https://cloud.r-project.org"
  )
)
```

## Example

The package includes simulated daily diary data. 100 participants reported
three variables (`var1`, `var2`, and `var3`) on 50 days. The data were simulated
so that all within-person correlations are positive and all between-person
correlations are negative.

```{r example, message = FALSE}
library(wbCorr)

data("simdat_intensive_longitudinal")
diary <- simdat_intensive_longitudinal[c("participantID", "var1", "var2", "var3")]

correlations <- wbCorr(diary, cluster = "participantID")
```

`summary()` shows both levels in one matrix. Within-person correlations are
above the diagonal, between-person correlations below it, and ICCs on the
diagonal.

```{r summary}
summary(correlations, "wb")
```

```{r values, include = FALSE}
within_r <- sprintf("%.2f", correlations@within$correlations["var1", "var2"])
between_r <- sprintf("%.2f", correlations@between$correlations["var1", "var2"])
```

For `var1` and `var2`, the two levels point in opposite directions. On days when
participants report a higher `var1` than usual, they also report a slightly
higher `var2` (r = `r within_r`). But participants with a higher average `var1`
have a lower average `var2` (r = `r between_r`).

`get_table()` returns the full results with test statistics, degrees of
freedom, confidence intervals, and p-values:

```{r table}
get_table(correlations)
```

`plot()` shows the data behind each correlation. The lower panels show
scatterplots with a regression line and outliers in red. The upper panels show
the correlation and its significance stars.

```{r within-plot, message = FALSE, fig.alt = "Scatterplot matrix of the within-person deviations of var1, var2, and var3, with the within-person correlations in the upper panels."}
plot(correlations, "within")
```

```{r between-plot, message = FALSE, fig.alt = "Scatterplot matrix of the person means of var1, var2, and var3, with the between-person correlations in the upper panels."}
plot(correlations, "between")
```

## Functions

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `wbCorr()` | Computes all correlations and ICCs. |
| `summary()`, `get_matrix()` | Correlation matrices with significance stars: within (`"w"`), between (`"b"`), or both in one matrix (`"wb"`, `"bw"`). |
| `get_table()` | Full tables with test statistics, confidence intervals, and p-values. |
| `get_ICC()` | ICC of each variable. |
| `plot()` | Scatterplot matrix of the within- or between-cluster parts. |
| `to_excel()` | Saves tables or matrices to an Excel file. |

## Options

| Argument | Options |
|---|---|
| `method` | `"pearson"` (default), `"spearman"`, or `"auto"` (Spearman for ordered factors, Pearson otherwise). |
| `inference` | `"analytic"` (default), `"cluster_bootstrap"`, or `"none"` (correlations only). |
| `between_weighting` | `"equal_clusters"` (default) weights each cluster equally. `"cluster_size"` weights each cluster by its number of observations of both variables. |
| `confidence_level` | Level of the confidence intervals (default: `0.95`). |
| `nboot` | Number of bootstrap samples (default: `1000`). |

For example, the cluster bootstrap resamples whole persons, so its confidence
intervals account for the dependence within persons:

```{r bootstrap}
set.seed(2026)
bootstrapped <- wbCorr(diary, cluster = "participantID", inference = "cluster_bootstrap")
get_table(bootstrapped, "between")
```

## How the correlations are computed

- Each variable is split into its cluster means (between part) and the
  deviations from these means (within part). Cluster means use all available
  observations of a variable, as in `psych::statsBy()`.
- Each correlation uses all rows where both variables are observed.
- Within-cluster correlations correlate the deviations. Tests use
  N - k - 1 degrees of freedom, where N is the number of complete pairs and k
  the number of clusters they come from. These tests treat the deviations as independent,
  which is an approximation. The cluster bootstrap does not make this
  assumption.
- Between-cluster correlations correlate the cluster means. Tests use
  k - 2 degrees of freedom.
- Pearson p-values use the t distribution. Spearman p-values and analytic
  confidence intervals use the Fisher z-transformation. The cluster bootstrap
  reports bias-corrected (BC) confidence intervals.
- The ICC is the ICC(1,1) of the one-way random-effects model, estimated from
  ANOVA mean squares.

Use numeric or binary variables. `wbCorr` converts ordered factors to their
level numbers; analyze them with `method = "auto"` or `"spearman"`. Dummy-code
nominal variables before use.

See `?wbCorr` for details.
